categories.name: Privacy / surveillance
categories.headline: image-capture offense
categories.basis: Iowa Code §715E.4 makes it a serious misdemeanor to fly a remotely piloted aircraft equipped with a surveillance device over another's homestead or farmstead (§715E.3 covers the same overflight without a device). https://www.legis.iowa.gov/docs/code/715E.pdf — Iowa criminalizes camera-drone overflights of homes and farms. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Trespass / airspace
categories.headline: altitude-threshold trespass
categories.basis: §715E.3 creates an overflight-intrusion offense keyed to the homestead footprint and a 400-ft horizontal "secured area" around farm animals/equipment/structures, and §715E.6(6) exempts any flight more than 400 ft above the earth's surface. https://www.legis.iowa.gov/docs/code/715E.pdf — Trespass is defined by a 400-ft horizontal farm buffer plus a 400-ft vertical safe harbor, not by a classic altitude ceiling over all private land. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Law-enforcement use
categories.headline: ban with exceptions
categories.basis: §321.492B flatly prohibits the state and its political subdivisions from using a UAV for traffic law enforcement (no exceptions in the codified text), and §808.15 makes UAV-obtained information inadmissible unless obtained under a search warrant or otherwise consistent with state/federal law. https://www.legis.iowa.gov/docs/code/2026/321.492B.pdf ; https://www.legis.iowa.gov/docs/code/2026/808.15.pdf — Iowa bans drone traffic enforcement outright and defaults to a warrant-or-lawful-collection evidence rule for other LE drone use; there is no freestanding LE warrant statute. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Government operators
categories.headline: none
categories.basis: No enacted permit/test or manufacturer rule for government drone operators was found; §715E.6(3) instead exempts government RPA use from the intrusion/surveillance offenses (a government-procurement ban exists only as introduced bill HF 2646). https://www.legis.iowa.gov/docs/code/715E.pdf — Government operators face no state drone permit, test, or approved-manufacturer rule. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Critical infrastructure
categories.headline: correctional only
categories.basis: §719.9 bans operating a UAV in, on, or above a county jail, municipal holding facility, secure juvenile facility, community-based correctional facility, or Dept. of Corrections institution and its contiguous grounds — Class "D" felony. https://www.legis.iowa.gov/docs/code/2026/719.9.pdf — Only correctional/custodial facilities get a drone-specific protection statute; no general critical-infrastructure drone offense is enacted. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Emergency scenes
categories.headline: none found

Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: State registration / permit
categories.headline: none

categories.name: Other conduct offenses
categories.headline: Free list
categories.basis: (i) Operating a UAV over a correctional facility — §719.9, Class "D" felony. (ii) State/local use of a UAV for traffic enforcement — §321.492B (prohibition on government, no stated penalty). (iii) Hunting from aircraft — §481A.120, aircraft-general, not drone-specific. No weaponized-drone statute found. https://www.legis.iowa.gov/docs/code/2026/719.9.pdf — Iowa's only drone-specific conduct crime outside ch. 715E is the prison/jail overflight felony. categories.name: Remedies & penalties
categories.headline: Free list
categories.basis: §715E.3: simple misdemeanor, serious misdemeanor on prior §715E.3/§715E.4 conviction. §715E.4: serious misdemeanor, aggravated misdemeanor on prior conviction. §715E.5: civil injunctive relief (temporary injunction ≤ 2 years, continuable), court costs, reasonable attorney fees, investigation/adjudication expenses, and court-ordered destruction of recordings made in violation. §719.9: Class "D" felony. §808.15: evidence exclusion. No statutory damages figure anywhere. https://www.legis.iowa.gov/docs/code/715E.pdf — Penalties climb a misdemeanor ladder, with injunctions, fees, and destruction of illegal recordings for farm/home victims. categories.name: Privacy / surveillance
categories.headline: image-capture offense
categories.basis: KRS 500.130(12) bars any person operating under subsections (3)–(5) from using a UAS to record an image of privately owned real property or of its owner/tenant/occupant/invitee/licensee with intent to conduct surveillance on, or publish unauthorized images of, the person/property in violation of a reasonable expectation of privacy (presumed where the property is not observable from ground level by someone lawfully present). Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Trespass / airspace
categories.headline: express airspace trespass
categories.basis: KRS 511.100(2)(b) makes it trespass upon key infrastructure assets to knowingly use a UAS to fly above real property containing a key infrastructure asset with intent to cause harm/damage or conduct surveillance, without the prior consent of the owner/tenant/lessee — an express overflight trespass, but only over listed infrastructure property, with no altitude threshold; general private-property airspace trespass is otherwise silent. https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/recorddocuments/bill/25RS/SB64/SCS1.pdf — Kentucky criminalizes drone overflight only over key-infrastructure land. categories.name: Law-enforcement use
categories.headline: warrant + exceptions
categories.basis: KRS 500.130(6): no LE agency or agent shall use a UAS to conduct a search unless authorized under the Fourth Amendment and Section 10 of the Kentucky Constitution, and if a warrant is used it shall specifically authorize the use of a UAS; (7) otherwise any government agency may use UAS for legitimate governmental purposes. https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/statutes/statute.aspx?id=56115 — Police drone searches need constitutional authorization, and a warrant must name the drone. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Government operators
categories.headline: none

Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.basis: KRS 511.100 is a general key-infrastructure trespass offense with two express UAS prongs — (2)(b) overflight with harmful/surveillance intent, and (2)(c) operating a UAS or recording/distributing images of procedures at assets listed in (1)(a)12–14 — and correctional facilities (state prison, juvenile justice facility, jail, detention facility grounds) are themselves asset item (1)(a)8 in the same list, so CI and correctional coverage live in one statute rather than a separate correctional-only law. https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/recorddocuments/bill/25RS/SB64/SCS1.pdf — One statute covers both power plants and prisons for drone trespass. Verified 2026-10-23 (official enacted-bill text; statute page UNREAD — see detail).

categories.name: Other conduct offenses
categories.headline: Free list
categories.basis: (i) Weaponized drones: KRS 500.130(2) — a UAS may not be equipped with a lethal payload, except UAS operated by the U.S. armed forces, reserve components, or Army/Air National Guard. (ii) Any crime by drone: KRS 501.110 — a person is guilty of an offense committed with the aid of a UAS under their control if the conduct would be criminal done directly (safe harbor: merely flying through navigable airspace in the normal course of operating a legally registered UAS). (iii) Hunting/fishing: 301 KAR 3:140 — a person shall not use an aircraft or UAS to fish, hunt, or take wildlife, drive/herd wildlife for taking, or harass wildlife (admin regulation, with department/landowner/invasive-carp exceptions). (iv) Airport interference / reckless operation: KRS 183.086 (UNREAD text; penalty verified via KRS 183.990(4)) — incursion into commercial-airport facility-map prohibited areas and reckless operation creating risk of serious injury/property damage. (v) Contraband delivery: covered generically by KRS 501.110; a drones-as-"dangerous contraband" definition in KRS 520.010 is an UNREAD lead (below). https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/statutes/statute.aspx?id=56115 ; https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/Statutes/statute.aspx?id=47514 ; https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/kar/titles/301/003/140/ — Kentucky bans lethal payloads outright and makes any crime committed by drone punishable as if done in person. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Remedies & penalties
categories.headline: Free list
categories.basis: KRS 411.067 civil action for violation of §500.130(12): injunctive relief, actual damages, punitive damages, court costs, reasonable attorney's fees (no statutory-damages figure); KRS 413.2475: 7-year limitations period. KRS 500.130(11): operating in violation of subsection (3) or (4) = a violation (first offense), Class B misdemeanor (second/subsequent). KRS 500.130(9): evidence obtained/collected by UAS is inadmissible in civil, criminal, or administrative proceedings to enforce state/local law, except evidence collected as permitted by (3)–(7) or offered against the UAS owner/operator for misconduct. KRS 511.100(3): Class B misdemeanor first offense, Class A misdemeanor second/subsequent. KRS 183.990(4): violating §183.086 = Class A misdemeanor, or Class D felony if it causes a significant change of course or serious disruption to an aircraft's safe travel threatening passengers/crew. KRS 512.020 criminal mischief 1st degree (Class D felony) reaches damaging a key infrastructure asset (not drone-specific). https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/Statutes/statute.aspx?id=56116 ; https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/statutes/statute.aspx?id=56117 ; https://apps.legislature.ky.gov/law/statutes/statute.aspx?id=56097 — Kentucky pairs a punitive-damages civil action with evidence exclusion and misdemeanor ladders. Carve-outs: lawful takeoff/landing flight paths; FAA-authorized commercial operation (other privacy/trespass actions preserved)

categories.name: Law-enforcement use
categories.headline: Ban with exceptions
categories.detail: Ban with exceptions — an LE agency may not operate a UAS, acquire information through one, or disclose UAS-acquired information except as §§ 837.310–.345 allow: warrant (max 30 days, renewable) or probable cause + exigent circumstances; written consent of the individual (about that individual/their property); search and rescue; documented emergency assistance (sworn statement to the circuit court within 48 hours); declared-emergency use for public-safety/property/damage-assessment purposes in the proclaimed area; specific crime/accident-scene reconstruction (max 5 days); training. Information acquired in violation is inadmissible, may not be disclosed in any adjudicatory proceeding, and may not establish reasonable suspicion or probable cause

categories.name: Government operators
categories.headline: Permit/test (registration form)
categories.detail: Permit/test (registration form) — a public body (other than an educational institution) may not operate a UAS in Oregon airspace without registering the UAS with the Oregon Department of Aviation; educational institutions register as users (no per-aircraft registration, no fee); the department maintains the registry and charges cost-recovery fees; unregistered-use evidence is inadmissible and cannot establish suspicion/probable cause

General aircraft law also bars landing on highways/public parks/public grounds without permission except in emergency (§ 837.090, pre-drone)

categories.headline: Weaponized UAS (§ 837
categories.detail: Weaponized UAS (§ 837.365): operating a UAS capable of firing a bullet/projectile, or designed/modified to cause and presently capable of causing serious physical injury — Class A misdemeanor; Class C felony if it fires; Class B felony if firing/design causes serious physical injury (nonlethal-projectile, FAA-authorized nonrecreational, noticed-and-insured, and educational exceptions; crowd-management use barred outright). Reckless interference with aircraft (§ 837.374): directing a laser at, crashing into, or preventing takeoff/landing of an aircraft. Interference with / unauthorized control of a government/LE/military/FAA-licensed UAS (§§ 837.375, 837.995(2)). Firing at an aircraft (§ 837.995(1), Class A felony). Flying over / photographing military or naval establishments without the commander's written permission (§ 837.095, general aircraft law)

categories.basis: § 423.009: a political subdivision may not adopt or enforce any ordinance, order, or measure regarding UA operation except for (1) special-event use, (2) the subdivision's own UA use, and (3) use near a facility/infrastructure the subdivision owns, if it obtains FAA authorization and holds a public hearing after reasonable notice; violating measures are void and unenforceable. VERIFIED–FULL TEXT. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: State registration / permit
categories.headline: none
categories.basis: No state drone registration or operator permit found in Ch. 423 (read in full); Transportation Code Ch. 24 aircraft provisions are manned-aircraft/federal-registration provisions, not a state drone registry. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Other conduct offenses
categories.headline: see detail
categories.basis: § 423.0046 sports-venue overflight ≤400 ft (venues seating ≥30,000) = Class B/A; Penal Code § 38.115 correctional/detention overflight, contact, or interference = Class B/A, state jail felony if used to provide/introduce contraband; hunting — using drones to hunt, drive, capture, take, count, or photograph wildlife is unlawful except under TPWD permits (31 TAC §§ 65.151–65.152 framework; Aerial Management Permit + Land Owner Authorization). No weaponized-drone statute found in Ch. 423. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Remedies & penalties
categories.headline: see detail
categories.basis: Criminal: § 423.003 Class C; § 423.004 possession Class C / disclosure etc. Class B, each image a separate offense; §§ 423.0045/423.0046 Class B, Class A on prior conviction; § 38.115 Class B/A, state jail felony for contraband. Civil: § 423.006 — owner/tenant may sue to enjoin and recover a $5,000 civil penalty per episode (§ 423.003) or $10,000 per episode (§ 423.004), or actual damages if disclosed with malice; prevailing party gets costs and reasonable attorney's fees; 2-year limitations. Evidence: § 423.005 bars use of unlawfully captured images as evidence and exempts them from disclosure/discovery, except to prove a Ch. 423 violation. VERIFIED–FULL TEXT. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Government data rules
categories.headline: none found (retention)
categories.basis: No retention/destruction rule for government drone data found in Ch. 423; § 423.008 requires public biennial use reports (Jan 1–15 of each odd-numbered year) from state LE agencies and from county/municipal LE agencies in jurisdictions over 150,000 population. VERIFIED–FULL TEXT. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Exception breadth
categories.headline: broad enumerated list
categories.detail: broad enumerated list — 21 lawful-capture situations in § 423.002(a)(1)–(21), plus 9 exemptions in § 423.0045(c) and 8 in § 423.0046(c)
categories.basis: VERIFIED–FULL TEXT. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Privacy / surveillance
categories.headline: none drone-specific (no drone image-capture offense found
categories.detail: none drone-specific (no drone image-capture offense found; protection runs through criminal trespass, § 76-6-206, and the LE data rules)
categories.basis: Title 72 Ch. 10 and § 76-6-206 were searched/read; no Utah drone-specific image-capture or surveillance offense for private parties was found. General voyeurism sections (§§ 76-12-306–309, referenced inside § 76-6-206) were not opened — UNREAD. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Trespass / airspace
categories.headline: express airspace trespass
categories.detail: express airspace trespass — no altitude threshold
categories.basis: § 76-6-206: "enter" includes intrusion of the entire unmanned aircraft; a UA "remains unlawfully" when it remains on or over private property not open to the public and the operator is not otherwise authorized to fly over it; causing a UA to enter and remain unlawfully over property with the listed intent/notice elements = criminal trespass (Class B; Class A in a dwelling). VERIFIED–FULL TEXT. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Law-enforcement use
categories.headline: warrant + exceptions
categories.basis: § 72-10-802: an LE agency/officer may not obtain, receive, or use UAS data unless obtained under a search warrant, a judicially recognized warrant exception, from a nongovernment actor (subject to limits), to locate a lost/missing individual in an area with no reasonable expectation of privacy, or in a manner that does not violate a reasonable expectation of privacy. Plus Part 8 documentation (§ 72-10-804). VERIFIED–FULL TEXT. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Government operators
categories.headline: approved-manufacturer list (scoped)
categories.basis: Part 12, §§ 72-10-1201–1202 (eff. 1/1/2025): a public entity, or a contractor working directly for one, may not purchase or operate a UAS for the inspection of critical infrastructure if manufactured/assembled by a covered foreign entity — a restriction scoped to CI-inspection use only, not a general fleet ban. VERIFIED–FULL TEXT (§ 1202); § 1201 VERIFIED–OFFICIAL SUMMARY. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Critical infrastructure
categories.headline: both
categories.basis: § 72-10-1002(6): no operation over any surface critical infrastructure facility (as defined in § 76-6-106.3) without the facility's prior authorization (exceptions: first responders; state/federal agencies with regulatory authority over the facility). Correctional facilities covered separately: § 72-10-903 (carry/drop or removal of items = third-degree felony; interference with operations/security = Class B misdemeanor). VERIFIED–FULL TEXT. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Emergency scenes
categories.headline: statute
categories.basis: § 65A-3-2.5: no operating a UAS within an FAA wildland-fire TFR or a designated wildland-fire scene without the incident commander's permission and compliance with the IC's restrictions; the IC or the jurisdiction's chief law-enforcement officer may neutralize a violating UA. § 72-10-1002 also bars operation violating a NOTAM. VERIFIED–FULL TEXT. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Takeoff / landing
categories.headline: park ban (rule)
categories.basis: Utah Admin. Code R651-602-8: a person must obtain written permission from the park manager before operating an unmanned aircraft within the state park system (authorizing law § 79-4-501). VERIFIED–FULL TEXT (official rules bulletin). Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Local preemption
categories.headline: state preempts
categories.basis: § 72-10-701 (eff. 5/3/2023): a political subdivision may not enact a law, ordinance, or rule governing the private use of an unmanned aircraft or advanced air mobility system unless authorized by Ch. 10, or the subdivision is an airport operator regulating operations within the airport's geographic boundaries or takeoff/landing at its airport; the chapter supersedes subdivision enactments predating July 1, 2022. § 65A-3-2.5(7) separately bars subdivisions from regulating private UA use in relation to a wildland fire. VERIFIED–FULL TEXT. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: State registration / permit
categories.headline: active (narrow
categories.detail: active (narrow — commercial, federally certificated operations only)
categories.basis: § 72-10-109(4): beginning January 1, 2025, a person may not operate in Utah a UAS or AAM aircraft for a commercial operation for which certification is required under federal rule unless the aircraft has a current state certificate of registration; § 72-10-110 directs UDOT rulemaking for a UAS/AAM registration fee and classification system. Recreational/private UAS are not state-registered. VERIFIED–FULL TEXT (§ 109); § 110 VERIFIED–OFFICIAL SUMMARY. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Other conduct offenses
categories.headline: see detail
categories.basis: § 72-10-902 weaponized UA (Class B misdemeanor); § 72-10-903 correctional carry/drop/removal (third-degree felony) and interference (Class B); § 65A-3-2.5 wildland-fire intrusion (tiered, see Cat. 11); § 76-13-214 harassment of livestock through use of a UAS (Class B/A); § 76-2-106 — an actor may be found guilty of an offense committed with the aid of a UA under the actor's control. VERIFIED–FULL TEXT. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Remedies & penalties
categories.headline: see detail
categories.basis: § 65A-3-2.5 tiered fire penalties: reckless violation by a non-government actor = Class B misdemeanor (fine ≤$2,500); Class A (≤$5,000) if it causes a firefighting aircraft to drop its payload in the wrong location, land without dropping, or be prevented from taking flight; third-degree felony (≤$10,000) on direct physical contact with a manned aircraft; second-degree felony (≤$15,000) if the UA's operation proximately causes a manned aircraft to collide with the ground, a structure, or another manned aircraft; restitution available. § 72-10-1002(9): violator liable for damages; written warning for a first violation, then infraction, then Class B misdemeanor per conviction. § 76-6-206(5)–(6): trespass carries statutory damages of the greater of 3× actual damages or $500, plus attorney fees up to $250 and costs, collectible in a separate civil action. VERIFIED–FULL TEXT. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Government data rules
categories.headline: retention limits
categories.basis: § 72-10-802: UAS data shall be destroyed as soon as reasonably possible, subject to the applicable retention schedule under Title 63G Ch. 2 (GRAMA) or other law. § 72-10-803: an agency may not use, copy, or disclose data collected on a non-target person/structure/area and must ensure it is destroyed as soon as reasonably possible, subject to five exceptions. § 72-10-804: encounter-record documentation of UAS use and data acquired. VERIFIED–FULL TEXT. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Exception breadth
categories.headline: moderate
categories.basis: Enumerated but bounded carve-outs: 5 data routes in § 72-10-802(1); 5 data-retention exceptions in § 72-10-803(2); 3 weapon exceptions in § 72-10-902(2); the § 72-10-702 carve-out for legitimate educational/business use conducted consistently with FAA rules; sanctioned-entity access list in § 65A-3-2.5. VERIFIED–FULL TEXT. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Privacy / surveillance
categories.headline: consent-based ban
categories.basis: 20 V.S.A. § 4626(b) bars recording an image of private property/owner/occupant without prior written consent with intent to conduct surveillance violating a reasonable expectation of privacy; civil penalty (see detail). https://legislature.vermont.gov/statutes/section/20/205/04626 — Plain note: You may not use a drone to surveil someone on their own land, where they expect privacy, without written permission first. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Trespass / airspace
categories.headline: altitude-threshold trespass
categories.basis: 20 V.S.A. § 4626(a): hobby/recreational flight below 100 ft above privately owned real property requires prior written consent of the owner. General background (not drone-specific): 5 V.S.A. § 402 vests ownership of airspace in the surface owner, subject to the § 403 right of flight. https://legislature.Vermont.gov/statutes/fullchapter/05/013 — Plain note: For hobby flying, 100 feet over someone else's land is Vermont's consent line. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Law-enforcement use
categories.headline: ban with exceptions
categories.basis: 20 V.S.A. § 4622(a)–(c): LE may not use a drone (or its information) to investigate/detect/prosecute crime except for non-crime purposes, under a Rule 41 warrant, or under a judicially recognized warrant exception; § 4622(d)(3) requires a warrant within 48 hours after exigent use begins. https://legislature.vermont.gov/statutes/fullchapter/20/205 — Plain note: Vermont police generally cannot use drones for criminal investigation unless an exception applies or they get a warrant — fast after the fact in a true emergency. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Government operators
categories.headline: none
categories.basis: 20 V.S.A. § 4623 requires all drone use (any person, including LE) to comply with FAA requirements/guidelines; no state permit, test, or approved-manufacturer list for government operators was found in ch. 205 or in searches of the Statutes Online. https://legislature.vermont.gov/statutes/fullchapter/20/205 — Plain note: Vermont adds no state operator credential on top of the FAA's. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Critical infrastructure
categories.headline: correctional only
categories.basis: 20 V.S.A. § 4625 prohibits knowingly operating a drone over a correctional facility / recognizable facility property (civil penalty up to $500). No general critical-infrastructure drone offense was found; searches covered ch. 205 (the complete drone chapter, §§ 4621–4626) and "critical infrastructure" terms. Correctional facilities are covered — separately, in § 4625, not as part of a CI statute. https://legislature.vermont.gov/statutes/fullchapter/20/205 — Plain note: Prisons are protected; Vermont has no broader drone-specific critical-infrastructure crime in its drone chapter. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Emergency scenes
categories.headline: none found
categories.basis: No drone-specific emergency-scene interference statute found in the Vermont Statutes Online (searched ch. 205 full text and drone/emergency terms). § 4622(c)(1) affirmatively permits LE assessment of accidents, forest fires and other fire scenes, flood stages, and storm damage — a permission, not a restriction on private operators. https://legislature.vermont.gov/statutes/fullchapter/20/205 — Plain note: Vermont restricts police at fire scenes less than it restricts them in investigations; it does not separately criminalize private drones at emergency scenes. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Takeoff / landing
categories.headline: consent statute
categories.basis: 20 V.S.A. § 4626 (consent, above); 5 V.S.A. § 403 makes landing an aircraft on another's land/water without consent unlawful except forced landing (general aircraft law, not drone-specific). Agency layer (procedure, not statute): VT Agency of Natural Resources procedure prohibits drone use originating/terminating on State Park and State Forest lands/facilities unless written Commissioner permission via Special Use Permit or License. https://anr.vermont.gov/dec/sites/anr/files/documents/Drones_on_State_Lands_Procedure_REVISED_FINAL.pdf — Plain note: Consent is the theme — from the landowner for low hobby flight and landing, and from the Commissioner for state park/forest land. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Local preemption
categories.headline: silent
categories.basis: No drone preemption or local-authority provision found in 20 V.S.A. ch. 205 (read in full) or in Statutes Online searches for drone/municipal terms. https://legislature.vermont.gov/statutes/fullchapter/20/205 — Plain note: Vermont's drone chapter says nothing about whether towns can add their own drone rules. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: State registration / permit
categories.headline: none
categories.basis: No state drone registration or operator permit found in ch. 205 or Statutes Online searches. § 4626(c) only requires drone sellers to give buyers written notice of § 4626(a)–(b), and references drones "required to be registered by the U.S. Department of Transportation" — i.e., federal registration, not a Vermont one. No repealed Vermont registration law was found. https://legislature.vermont.gov/statutes/section/20/205/04626 — Plain note: There is no Vermont drone registration; the only notice duty falls on sellers. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Other conduct offenses
categories.headline: weaponized drones; aerial hunting; correctional overflight
categories.detail: weaponized drones; aerial hunting; correctional overflight
categories.basis: (i) 13 V.S.A. § 4018 — equipping a drone with a dangerous/deadly weapon or firing a projectile from a drone. (ii) 10 V.S.A. App. § 20 (Fish & Wildlife Board "Aerial Hunting" rule) — purpose stated on the official host is "to restrict the taking of wild animals by use of aircraft and drones." (iii) 20 V.S.A. § 4625 — correctional overflight (also Cat. 5). URLs in detail below. Plain note: Vermont separately bans armed drones and restricts using aircraft/drones to take wild animals. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Remedies & penalties
categories.headline: civil penalties (§§ 4625, 4626)
categories.detail: civil penalties (§§ 4625, 4626); criminal penalty (§ 4018); evidence exclusion + destruction (§ 4622)
categories.basis: § 4626(d): civil penalty ≤$50 first / ≤$250 subsequent violation. § 4625(b): civil penalty ≤$500. § 4018: imprisonment ≤1 year and/or fine ≤$1,000. § 4622(e): information/evidence gathered in violation is inadmissible in any judicial or administrative proceeding; § 4622(d)(3)(B): if a post-hoc warrant is denied, use ceases immediately and gathered information/evidence is destroyed. No drone-specific statutory-damages civil action found. Plain note: Vermont's sharpest remedy is evidentiary — break the police-drone rules and the evidence is excluded and, in the denied-warrant case, destroyed. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Government data rules
categories.headline: none found (no fixed retention period)
categories.basis: 20 V.S.A. § 4622(d)(1)–(2) requires target-only collection and bars facial recognition / biometric matching on anyone other than the target; § 4622(d)(3)(B) requires destruction when a post-hoc warrant is denied; § 4624 requires annual LE reporting (uses, investigations/arrests aided, non-target data collected, cost/funding) to the Dept. of Public Safety and on to the House/Senate Judiciary and Government Operations Committees. No fixed retention-day limit appears in the chapter text read. https://legislature.vermont.gov/statutes/fullchapter/20/205 — Plain note: Vermont limits what police drones may collect and forces yearly public reporting, but sets no "delete after X days" clock in the statute. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Exception breadth
categories.headline: moderate
categories.basis: § 4622(c) has 2 main LE routes (non-crime purpose; warrant/judicial exception), plus the § 4622(b)(2) observational carve-outs. § 4625(c) lists 6 exempt categories (3 outright, 3 with prior notice). § 4626(f) lists 2 exemptions (utilities/contractors; LE). Counted: 2 LE routes + 6 correctional + 2 private-property exemptions. Plain note: Exceptions are enumerated and mission-specific, not open-ended. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Privacy / surveillance
categories.headline: image-capture offense
categories.basis: Va. Code § 18.2-324.2 makes it a Class 1 misdemeanor for a person required to register under § 9.1-901, or a protective-order respondent (§§ 16.1-279.1 / 19.2-152.10), to use a UAS to follow/contact another person without permission or capture recognizable images of them without permission. No general (all-persons) drone peeping/surveillance statute was found; the general privacy protection is the trespass statute in Cat. 2. https://law.lis.virginia.gov/vacode/title18.2/chapter7/section18.2-324.2/ — Plain note: Virginia's drone image-capture crime is aimed at registered sex offenders and people under protective orders, not at everyone. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Trespass / airspace
categories.headline: altitude-threshold trespass
categories.basis: Va. Code § 18.2-121.3(A)(i): knowingly/intentionally causing a UAS to enter another's property and come within 50 feet of a dwelling house (a) to coerce, intimidate, or harass, or (b) after actual notice to desist, for any other reason — Class 1 misdemeanor. Note: the 50 feet is a proximity-to-dwelling measure as written, not a floor/ceiling altitude. https://law.lis.virginia.gov/vacode/title18.2/chapter5/section18.2-121.3/ — Plain note: Getting a drone within 50 feet of someone's house to harass them — or after being told to stop — is a crime in Virginia. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Law-enforcement use
categories.headline: warrant + exceptions
categories.basis: Va. Code § 19.2-60.1(B): state/local LE and regulatory-enforcement bodies may use a UAS only during execution of a search warrant or administrative/inspection warrant; § 19.2-60.1(C) lists 11 warrantless exceptions (i)–(xi). https://law.lis.virginia.gov/vacode/title19.2/chapter5/section19.2-60.1/ — Plain note: Virginia police need a warrant to fly a drone for enforcement, with a long list of specific exceptions. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Government operators
categories.headline: none
categories.basis: § 19.2-60.1(D) takes non-law-enforcement government support uses (damage, traffic, flood stage, wildfire assessment) outside the warrant requirement; no state permit, test, or approved-manufacturer list for government operators was found in the Code/VAC searches. https://law.lis.virginia.gov/vacode/title19.2/chapter5/section19.2-60.1/ — Plain note: Non-police agencies fly for assessment work without a state drone credential. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Critical infrastructure
categories.headline: both
categories.basis: § 18.2-121.3(B): unauthorized UAS entry into airspace over public services/utilities (§ 18.2-162), critical infrastructure as defined in 42 U.S.C. § 5195c (including DoD military bases), or MTSA facilities (46 U.S.C. § 70101) — Class 4 felony. Correctional facilities are covered separately in § 18.2-121.3(A)(iii) (dropping any item within, or imaging an identifiable inmate/resident of, a state/local correctional facility or juvenile correctional center — Class 1 misdemeanor), and contracted defense facilities in § 18.2-121.3(D) (imaging controlled technical information — Class 4 felony). https://law.lis.virginia.gov/vacode/title18.2/chapter5/section18.2-121.3/ — Plain note: Flying over power/utilities, critical infrastructure, or a military base without authorization is a felony; prisons and defense plants have their own drone rules in the same section. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Emergency scenes
categories.headline: statute
categories.basis: Va. Code § 27-15.1: the fire chief / officer in charge at a fire, explosion, or hazardous-materials emergency has authority to maintain order at the incident and its vicinity "including the immediate airspace"; refusing the chief's orders is a Class 4 misdemeanor. https://law.lis.virginia.gov/vacodefull/title27/ — Plain note: At a Virginia fire or hazmat scene, the fire chief controls the airspace right over the incident — disobeying is a crime. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Takeoff / landing
categories.headline: park ban (rule)
categories.basis: 4VAC5-30-400 (Virginia State Parks Regulations): "No person shall voluntarily land or unlawfully operate within or upon any park" any airplane, remote-control model aircraft, helicopter, unmanned aerial system, drone, etc.; forced landings excepted; rescue/evacuation aircraft exempt for emergencies and approved training. Plus § 15.2-926.3(B) (Cat. 8) for local takeoff/landing rules on subdivision-owned property. https://law.lis.virginia.gov/admincode/title4/agency5/chapter30/section400/ — Plain note: State parks are effectively no-drone areas under the parks regulation, emergencies aside. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Local preemption
categories.headline: partial (launch/recovery or own property)
categories.basis: Va. Code § 15.2-926.3(A): no political subdivision may regulate the use of a privately owned UAS within its boundaries. § 15.2-926.3(B): a subdivision may, by ordinance/regulation developed under Dept. of Aviation rules, regulate takeoff and landing of unmanned aircraft on property the subdivision owns (with reporting to the Department, which publishes an annual summary); § 15.2-926.3(D) bars construing that power to prohibit FAA-compliant commercial takeoff/landing, emergency/maintenance operations, malfunction landings, sworn public-safety officers, and U.S. government operations. https://law.lis.virginia.gov/vacode/title15.2/chapter9/section15.2-926.3/ — Plain note: Towns can't regulate drone use, but they can regulate taking off and landing on their own land, under state aviation rules. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: State registration / permit
categories.headline: none
categories.basis: Va. Code § 5.1-5(A) expressly provides: "Any owner of an unmanned aircraft as defined in § 19.2-60.1 shall not be required to register such aircraft" under Virginia's aircraft-registration law. No state operator permit found. No repealed drone registration was found — the exemption is affirmative and current in the text read. https://law.lis.virginia.gov/vacodefull/title5.1/chapter1/ — Plain note: Virginia law says outright that drone owners do not have to register their aircraft with the state. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Other conduct offenses
categories.headline: sex-offender/protective-order use (§ 18
categories.detail: sex-offender/protective-order use (§ 18.2-324.2); correctional drop/image (§ 18.2-121.3(A)(iii)); FAA security-restriction takeoff/landing (§ 18.2-121.3(A)(ii)); hunting (4VAC15-20-240; § 5.1-17); government weaponized UAS (§ 19.2-60.1(F))
categories.basis: § 18.2-121.3(A)(ii): takeoff/landing violating FAA Special Security Instructions / UAS Security Sensitive Airspace Restrictions — Class 1 misdemeanor. 4VAC15-20-240: unlawful to use a drone/UAS to hunt, take, or kill a wild animal, drive/herd wildlife for hunting, locate/surveil/assist hunting, or harass a wild animal; also unlawful to hunt the same calendar day on a property after using a drone to locate/surveil a wild animal there in open season (Dept. wildlife-management and specified government uses excepted). § 5.1-17: hunting from an aircraft in flight is a misdemeanor (general aircraft law). § 19.2-60.1(F): no weaponized UAS may be deployed in the Commonwealth, or its use facilitated, by a state/local government body — except operations at the Space Port and Naval/Aegis facilities at Wallops Island; counter-UAS systems designed to disable another UAS are excluded from "weaponized." URLs in detail below. Plain note: Virginia piles up specific drone offenses — hunting, prison drops/images, security-zone takeoffs, and a flat ban on government weaponized drones outside Wallops Island. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Remedies & penalties
categories.headline: Class 1 misdemeanor (§§ 18
categories.detail: Class 1 misdemeanor (§§ 18.2-121.3(A), 18.2-324.2); Class 4 felony (§ 18.2-121.3(B), (D)); Class 4 misdemeanor (§ 27-15.1); evidence exclusion (§ 19.2-60.1(E)); counter-drone immunity (§ 18.2-121.3(D))
categories.basis: § 19.2-60.1(E): evidence obtained by UAS in violation of the section "is not admissible in any criminal or civil proceeding." § 18.2-121.3(D): a contracted defense facility's owner/operator and employees are immune from criminal prosecution and civil liability for preventing/stopping/deterring/interrupting/repelling a UAS entering the facility property, if no person is injured. No drone-specific statutory-damages civil action was found in the sections read. Plain note: Virginia pairs felony/misdemeanor penalties with automatic evidence exclusion for warrant violations and a self-help immunity for defense plants. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Government data rules
categories.headline: none found
categories.basis: No retention limit, deletion deadline, or drone-data reporting duty appears in § 19.2-60.1 as read in full, and none was found in Code searches for UAS data/retention terms. (Contrast VT § 4624 reporting and WA's unenacted bills.) https://law.lis.virginia.gov/vacode/title19.2/chapter5/section19.2-60.1/ — Plain note: Virginia controls when police may fly, and excludes illegally obtained evidence, but sets no state clock for deleting drone data. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Exception breadth
categories.headline: broad enumerated list
categories.basis: § 19.2-60.1(C) enumerates 11 warrantless-deployment clauses, (i)–(xi): Amber Alert; Senior Alert; Blue Alert; immediate danger to any person; post-accident crash-reconstruction survey by LE/State Police/local LE; VDOT assisting LE crash reports; training exercises; consent; arrest-warrant residence survey / hot pursuit of a fleeing arrestee; LE investigation of UAS around/over federal or state government property, public critical infrastructure, or non-government prison/jail facilities; and Dept. of Environmental Quality civil enforcement against a permittee under specified Title 62.1 articles. Plus § 19.2-60.1(D) non-LE carve-out, (G) Armed Forces / VA National Guard carve-out, and § 18.2-121.3(C)'s 4 trespass exemptions. Counted: 11 + carve-outs. Plain note: This is one of the longest exception lists in any state drone law — read the exact clause before assuming a flight was warrantless-but-lawful. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Privacy / surveillance
categories.headline: none drone-specific
categories.basis: No drone-specific privacy/surveillance statute found in RCW searches for "unmanned." General law only: RCW 9A.44.115 (voyeurism) — knowingly viewing/photographing/filming another person without knowledge and consent, for the purpose of arousing/gratifying sexual desire, where the person has a reasonable expectation of privacy; voyeurism in the first degree is a class C felony. The statute does not mention drones. http://app.leg.wa.gov/RCW/default.aspx?cite=9A.44.115 — Plain note: Washington has no drone peeping law; a drone used for sexual voyeurism would be charged under the general voyeurism statute. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Trespass / airspace
categories.headline: silent
categories.basis: No drone airspace-trespass statute (express or altitude-threshold) found in RCW searches for "unmanned" / "unpiloted" — the only RCW aeronautics hit is the definition at RCW 47.68.020(21). No altitude threshold exists in Washington state drone law as found. https://apps.leg.wa.gov/rcw/default.aspx?cite=47.68.020 — Plain note: Washington state law does not set a height below which drone flight becomes trespass. Verified 2026-10-23.

categories.name: Law-enforcement use
categories.headline: none
categories.basis: No enacted LE drone statute (no warrant rule, ban, or reporting duty) found in the RCW.
